look_here_first: Start with the bark and spur shoots. Mexican plum is a small deciduous tree with gray to orange-brown bark, alternate simple serrate leaves, and clusters of fragrant white flowers on short lateral spur shoots. Then confirm the Rosaceae hypanthium, many free stamens, single superior ovary, and a glaucous purple-gray drupe.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: bark gray with horizontal lenticels on typical stems, becoming orange-brown and fissured on larger trunks

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaves alternate, simple, serrate, stipulate, often short-hairy/velvety when young

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: flowers in small umbel-like clusters on short lateral spur shoots

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: 5 white petals arising from the rim of a bell-shaped hypanthium

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: about 30 free stamens in several series

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: single superior one-chambered ovary with one ovule

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: fruit a round glaucous purple-gray drupe with a single stone

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Alternate simple leaves with early-deciduous stipules; blades broadly elliptic to ovate/obovate and serrate.

key_traits.label: Flower
key_traits.text: Five petals and many stamens arise from a conspicuous hypanthium; the single pistil sits free inside rather than being fused to the hypanthium.

key_traits.label: Fruit
key_traits.text: One superior ovary becomes one drupe with a single hard endocarp/stone.

key_traits.label: Family training
key_traits.text: Excellent Rosaceae comparison against Rubus trivialis: both show a hypanthium and many stamens, but Prunus has one carpel becoming one drupe while Rubus has many free carpels becoming an aggregate of drupelets.
